title: WWF-India Urges a Crackers-Free Diwali in Green Campaign to Nov 8
excerpt: WWF-India's EIACP centre launched a nationwide Green Diwali campaign from October 20 to November 8 urging citizens to avoid firecrackers, as Delhi entered the festival season with AQI already bordering on poor.
body:
• WWF-India's EIACP Programme Centre has launched a nationwide Green Diwali campaign running from October 20 to November 8, urging citizens to avoid firecrackers, according to The News Mill.
  • The campaign, supported by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change under Mission LiFE, promotes a cracker-free, plastic-free Diwali built on diyas, LED or solar lighting, natural rangoli and locally made gifts.
  • For your health: Delhi's AQI averaged 174.5 over October 1-4, 2026 — moderate bordering on poor, against 119.75 a year earlier — and CPCB classifies 201-300 as poor, when most people can face breathing discomfort; skipping crackers avoids adding PM2.5 on top of that baseline.
  • Diwali falls on November 8, 2026, the campaign's closing day — people with asthma or COPD, children and older adults should check the day's AQI, limit outdoor time when it is poor, and keep rescue inhalers accessible.

WWF-India's EIACP Programme Centre has launched a nationwide Green Diwali campaign urging citizens to avoid firecrackers, with the drive running from October 20 to November 8, the day Diwali is celebrated this year. The campaign asks households to keep the festival's light and ritual while dropping the smoke, noise and single-use waste that now accompany it.

What the campaign asks people to do

The Green Diwali campaign is run by WWF-India's EIACP (Environmental Information, Awareness, Capacity Building and Livelihood Programme) Centre, supported by the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, under Mission LiFE — the national programme that promotes everyday lifestyle choices that reduce environmental harm. The Press Information Bureau release for the campaign lists the specific swaps it promotes.

Replace plastic decorations with biodegradable or upcycled materials. Make rangoli from natural ingredients such as rice flour, flower petals and turmeric. Choose LED lights, solar lanterns or traditional earthen diyas to save energy. Buy locally made gifts and products to cut the carbon footprint. Avoid single-use plastics and minimise festive waste. Above all, the campaign invites citizens to take a pledge for a clean, green and plastic-free Diwali — and, in its current nationwide push, a cracker-free one.

The record it builds on

This is not a first attempt. The campaign builds on WWF EIACP's flagship 'Breath of Change – Clean Air, Blue Skies' initiative, which engaged more than 2,00,000 citizens across Delhi through 25 awareness programmes. In the previous Diwali season, the centre inaugurated a 'Breathable Art' installation in Rohini, in Delhi, intended to symbolise community action for clean air.

The initiative also ties into India's commitments under Sustainable Development Goal 12, on responsible consumption and production, and SDG 13, on climate action, according to the PIB release.

Why the air-quality backdrop matters this year

The appeal lands in a season when Delhi's air had already deteriorated before any firecrackers were lit. Monitoring reported for early October 2026 put Delhi's average AQI at 174.5 for October 1-4 — well above 119.75 in the same period in 2025 and 167.25 in 2024, and the highest for that window since 2020 apart from that year's 176.25 — with levels climbing to 187 by October 4, according to a clinical review of CPCB data.

Under the Central Pollution Control Board framework, an AQI of 101-200 is moderate and 201-300 is poor. Firecracker smoke is rich in PM2.5 — particles 2.5 micrometres or smaller that can travel deep into the lungs and into the bloodstream. Adding a night of cracker emissions to air that is already bordering on poor is the specific risk the campaign is trying to remove: the festival does not start from clean air.

What this means for families celebrating

For diaspora families marking Diwali on November 8 in the United States and elsewhere, the campaign's checklist travels well: diyas or LEDs instead of extra fireworks where local rules restrict them, natural rangoli materials, and gifts from local makers. For family in Delhi and other northern cities, the health steps are concrete — check CPCB AQI readings on the day, prefer a well-fitted N95 over a cloth mask outdoors when AQI is poor, keep windows closed during peak smoke, and make sure anyone with asthma or COPD has maintenance and rescue inhalers to hand.

The campaign runs through November 8. Whether it moves the post-Diwali AQI will be measurable in the CPCB readings for November 9 and 10 — the numbers WWF-India and the ministry will ultimately be judged against.
nri_angle: Diaspora families celebrating Diwali on November 8 can use the campaign's diya, LED and natural-rangoli swaps, while family in Delhi should follow the AQI and inhaler precautions.
author: Diaspora Desk
